title: Offences and Penalties and Ethical Aspects under GST
outcomes: Apply penalties under section 122 and the general penalty.
Compute penalties for goods in transit and confiscation.
Apply principles of penalty and ethical aspects.

meta.exam_tip: For section 129, first ask whether the owner came forward and whether goods are taxable.

concepts.title: Penalties under section 122 and general penalty
body: Section 122(1) lists 21 offences by taxable persons — e.g. supplying without invoice or with false invoice, issuing invoices without supply, collecting tax but not paying within three months, wrongly availing ITC or refund, not deducting or collecting tax, evading registration, obstructing officers, and dealing in goods liable to confiscation. Penalty is the higher of ₹10,000 (₹20,000 under IGST) and the tax evaded, ITC wrongly availed or refund wrongly obtained.

Section 122(1A) penalises any person who retains the benefit of or causes specified offences (fake invoices, wrongful ITC) with an amount equal to the tax evaded or ITC passed on. Section 122(1B) penalises ECOs for allowing supplies by unregistered or ineligible persons. Section 122(2) covers registered persons short paying tax for non-fraud (higher of ₹10,000 and 10% of tax) or fraud reasons (higher of ₹10,000 and tax).

Section 122(3) penalises those who aid, abet or deal in goods liable to confiscation with up to ₹25,000. Section 125 imposes a general penalty up to ₹25,000 for contraventions with no specific penalty. Section 122B (track and trace) penalises a person who breaches the track and trace mechanism of section 148A with an extra penalty of ₹1 lakh or 10% of tax payable on the goods, whichever is higher.
concepts.analogy: Penalties scale with tax evaded, with fixed minimums.
concepts.work: Issuing invoices without supply attracts penalty at least equal to ITC passed on.

concepts.title: Detention and confiscation of goods in transit
body: Section 129: goods and conveyances in transit in contravention of the law may be detained or seized and released on payment of penalty: if the owner comes forward, 200% of tax payable (for exempt goods, lower of 2% of value and ₹25,000); if the owner does not, the higher of 50% of value and 200% of tax (exempt goods: lower of 5% of value and ₹25,000). IGST amounts are doubled correspondingly.

A notice must be issued within seven days of detention and an order passed within seven days of notice; if penalty is not paid within 15 days of the order, the goods or conveyance may be sold or disposed of.

Section 130: goods or conveyances used to evade tax with intent are liable to confiscation; the owner may pay a fine in lieu of confiscation not exceeding market value minus tax, plus tax and penalty; a conveyance owner who did not know of its use may pay a fine equal to tax on the goods.
concepts.analogy: Transit violations cost 200% of tax or more.
concepts.work: Goods worth ₹5 lakh with ₹90,000 tax detained without bills can attract ₹2.5 lakh penalty if no owner appears.

concepts.title: Prosecution and compounding
body: Section 132: offences like supply without invoice, fake invoices, fraudulent ITC or refund are punishable with imprisonment up to 5 years (amount above ₹5 crore), 3 years (₹2–5 crore), 1 year (₹1–2 crore), plus fine; falsification and obstruction up to 6 months. Repeat offences carry up to 5 years. Offences above ₹5 crore under specified clauses are cognizable and non-bailable; others non-cognizable and bailable. Prosecution needs prior sanction of the Commissioner.

Section 138: offences (except specified serious ones and repeat cases) may be compounded by the Commissioner, before or after prosecution, on payment of a compounding amount between 25% and 100% of tax involved, as per rule 162, after paying tax, interest and penalty.

Compounding is not available to a person who has been allowed compounding earlier for certain offences, or who has committed specified offences (like supplying without invoice) above specified amounts.
concepts.analogy: Serious fraud may lead to prosecution; compounding offers settlement.
concepts.work: Fake ITC of ₹3 crore can attract imprisonment up to three years.

concepts.title: Principles of penalty and ethical aspects
body: Section 126: no penalty for minor breaches (tax involved below ₹5,000) or easily rectifiable procedural mistakes without fraudulent intent or gross negligence; penalty must depend on facts and be proportionate; a person must be heard and reasons recorded; voluntary disclosure is considered a mitigating factor.
Section 127 lets the officer impose penalty where it is not covered by other proceedings after giving a hearing. Section 128 enables waiver of penalty and late fee by notification.

Ethical aspects: professionals must avoid facilitating fake invoices, ensure correct ITC claims, and maintain integrity — misuse of GST for fraudulent ITC harms the system and attracts personal liability under section 122(1A).
concepts.analogy: Penalties must be fair, reasoned and proportionate.
concepts.work: A spelling error in an invoice with no tax effect should not be penalised.

summary: Section 122: 21 offences; higher of ₹10,000 and tax.
Section 129: 200%; higher of 50% of value and 200%.
remember: No penalty for minor breaches below ₹5,000.

viva.q: What is fine in lieu of confiscation?
viva.model: A fine up to market value minus tax, paid in addition to tax and penalty, to redeem confiscated goods.
The Commissioner must give prior sanction.

viva.q: What penalty applies to an ECO allowing ineligible suppliers?
viva.model: Under section 122(1B), the higher of ₹10,000 and the tax involved.

viva.q: Is voluntary disclosure relevant to penalty?
viva.model: Yes, section 126 treats it as a mitigating factor.

viva.q: What happens if penalty under section 129 is unpaid within 15 days of the order?
viva.model: The goods or conveyance may be sold or disposed of to recover the amount.
